section.title: Beware of Deceivers
section.sectionRationale: This is the heart and the sharp edge of the letter. Having urged love in the truth, the elder now warns that many deceivers deny that Jesus came in the flesh. He calls the readers to watch themselves, to abide in the teaching of Christ, and even to refuse hospitality and greeting to those who bring another gospel.
section.thesis: Because many deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh have gone out into the world, the readers must guard themselves, abide in the teaching of Christ that alone holds the Father and the Son, and refuse to lend aid or welcome to those who carry a Christ-denying message.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the deceivers and the antichrist; the call to watch and abide in Christ's teaching; the refusal of welcome to false teachers.

verses.text: For many {{planos|deceivers}} have gone out into the world, refusing to {{homologeo|confess}} the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the {{antichristos|antichrist}}.
Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully {{misthos|rewarded}}.
Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the {{didache|teaching}} of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.

units.label: No welcome for false teachers
units.note: do not receive or greet them

verses.text: If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him.
Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.

planos.gloss: A deceiver, one who leads astray, a wanderer who makes others wander. The same root gives the word for a wandering star or a vagrant. These are not honest strugglers but active misleaders who have gone out into the world to pull believers off the path of truth.

homologeo.gloss: To confess, acknowledge, or agree together with. It describes open, public confession of the truth about Jesus. The deceivers refuse to confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; the failure is not ignorance but a settled refusal to acknowledge the incarnate Son.

antichristos.gloss: Antichrist, one who stands against and in place of Christ. In John's letters the term names not only a final figure but the many present deniers of the incarnate Son. To reject that the Christ has truly come in the flesh is to embody the very spirit of antichrist.

misthos.gloss: Reward, wages, what is due for work done. The elder wants the readers to receive a full reward and not to forfeit what he and others have laboured for. It is not that salvation is earned, but that faithfulness carries a reward and defection carries loss.

didache.gloss: Teaching, instruction, doctrine. The teaching of Christ is the apostolic message about who Jesus is and what He has done, and perhaps also the teaching that comes from Him. To abide in it is to hold the Father and the Son; to run beyond it is to lose God altogether.

basic.context: Now the elder sounds the alarm. Travelling teachers were spreading through the churches who denied that Jesus really came in a human body. He calls them deceivers and antichrists. He warns the readers to watch themselves so they do not lose their reward, to hold fast to the true teaching about Christ, and not to help or even welcome those who carry the false message.
basic.hermeneutics: The hard verses are 10 and 11, where the elder says not to receive such a person into your home or even greet him. This is not a ban on ordinary kindness to outsiders; it is about not giving official welcome, hospitality, and support to travelling false teachers, which in that world meant endorsing and funding their mission. To greet them so is to share in their work of pulling people from Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The deceivers, planoi, are active misleaders. They refuse to confess, homologeo, that Jesus came in the flesh, which makes each of them the antichrist, antichristos. The elder wants the readers to keep their full reward, misthos, by abiding in the teaching, didache, of Christ, which alone holds the Father and the Son.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, but the pattern is old: as false prophets once led Israel astray, so now antichrists go out to deceive the church. The true teaching of Christ, in which believers abide, stands over against every counterfeit, as it always has.
basic.christ: The test is Jesus Himself: that the Christ has truly come in the flesh. The incarnation is not negotiable. To abide in the teaching of Christ is to have both the Father and the Son; to abandon it is to have neither. Christ, truly God and truly man, is the dividing line between having God and not having Him.
basic.god: God is known only through His Son as He truly is. There is no access to the Father that bypasses the incarnate Christ. God is also jealous for His people's safety, warning them plainly and calling them not to give aid to those who would rob them of Him.
basic.crossReferences: 1 John says the same, that denying Jesus come in the flesh is the spirit of antichrist. 3 John, by contrast, commends welcoming true travelling teachers, showing that hospitality itself is good; the issue is who is being welcomed.
basic.oneStory: The one story of Scripture centres on God come in the flesh in Jesus. To deny that is to strike at the heart of the gospel. The elder guards the young churches so that the truth about Christ, on which everything depends, is not traded away, and so God's people keep both the Father and the Son.

context.literary:
Verse 7 opens with 'for,' which makes the whole section the reason for what has gone before. The elder has urged love and obedient walking. Now he explains why that urgency cannot wait: there are people abroad who would unpick the very truth in which love stands. The five verses move in a clear arc. Verse 7 gives the situation, verse 8 the self-watch it demands, verse 9 the principle that divides the true from the false, verses 10 and 11 the practical consequence.

The paragraph is also a small study in pairs. 'Deceivers' who 'have gone out' stand against the elder and his friends who have laboured. The one who 'runs ahead' stands against the one who 'remains.' The one who 'does not have God' stands against the one who 'has both the Father and the Son.' The one who is not received stands against the church that must not receive him, and the one who 'greets' is set beside the one who 'shares.' John writes in such sharp opposites because he sees the choice that way.

Look too at how the verbs of work frame the unit. In verse 8 the elder speaks of what 'we have worked for,' and in verse 11 of the 'evil deeds' of the false teacher, using the related noun for works. The church's labour is set against the labour of the deceiver, and a careless welcome in verse 10 turns the household from partner in one work into partner in the other. This is the letter's turning point, and it is also where its tone changes from tender to stern. Yet the same vocabulary of truth and teaching that ran through verses 1 to 6 still runs here, so that the warning is not a new subject but the old subject under attack.
context.historical:
The late first century was a time of unsettled teaching. The apostles were dying, the churches were scattered across the cities of Asia Minor and beyond, and a number of travelling teachers carried their own versions of the gospel from house to house. First John tells us what had happened in John's own circle. Some who had belonged to the community 'went out from us,' 1 John 2:19, and were now teaching elsewhere, denying that Jesus is the Christ, 1 John 2:22, and that He has come in the flesh, 1 John 4:2-3. The letter we are reading is a warning about precisely such people.

The error is usually described as an early form of what later writers called docetism, the idea that the Christ only seemed to have a body, or as the related view that the divine Christ joined the man Jesus at His baptism and left before He died. A little later, Ignatius of Antioch opposed teachers who said that Christ had only appeared to suffer. John does not name a school. He gives a test, 'refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh,' that cuts through many versions of the idea. First John 5:6 insists that Jesus came 'by water and blood,' which may be aimed at the claim that the Christ was present only at the baptism and not at the cross.

The instruction of verses 10 and 11 makes sense in a world of travelling ministry. Teachers and prophets who moved between congregations expected lodging and support from the host families, and the early church manual known as the Didache, whose exact date is debated but which belongs to this early period, gives rules for testing and limiting such visitors. A house church that opened its door to a travelling teacher was giving him a platform, a hearing and the host's good name. The elder's counsel to withhold all of that from a teacher who denies the incarnation was a concrete act of protection for the congregation.
context.canonical:
The warning belongs to a long thread in Scripture about false teaching. Moses had told Israel to test every prophet by whether he led them toward other gods, Deuteronomy 13:1-5, and the prophets repeated the charge. Jesus warned that many would come in His name and deceive many, Matthew 24:4-5, and told His disciples to beware of false prophets in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that savage wolves would come in among them and that even from their own number men would rise up and distort the truth, Acts 20:29-30. The elder is writing to the same region, and his letter reads like a later chapter of the same story.

Within the Johannine writings, the verse is a close companion to 1 John. The word antichrist, found in the New Testament only in the letters of John, appears in 1 John 2:18, 2:22 and 4:3 as well as here. The test of confession in verse 7 echoes 1 John 4:2-3, and verse 9's claim that denying the Son means not having the Father repeats 1 John 2:23. Third John supplies the balance: Gaius is praised for supporting travelling workers, 3 John 5-8, while Diotrephes, who refuses to welcome the brothers, is rebuked in 3 John 9-10. Hospitality is a good thing in the New Testament, Hebrews 13:2, and the question of verses 10 and 11 is whom it serves.

Other apostles drew the same boundary. Paul says that anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one received is under a curse, Galatians 1:8-9, tells the Romans to watch out for those who create divisions contrary to the teaching they learned, Romans 16:17, and gives Titus a rule for a divisive person, Titus 3:10. Peter warns that false teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, 2 Peter 2:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants his readers to understand that the church faces a real danger and that it is a danger to the gospel itself. He does not treat the matter as a disagreement among friends. He names the deceivers plainly, ties them to the spirit of antichrist, and gives a simple test that any member of a household church could apply: does this person confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh?

He wants the readers to take responsibility. The verbs of verse 8 are plural commands addressed to the whole group: watch yourselves. He is not asking them to wait for a leader to rescue them, and he is not telling them to hand the matter to him. The danger is that they could lose what has been built, and the guarding of it belongs to them.

He also wants them to understand how to respond practically. The test of verse 9 is about teaching, not temperament, and the response of verses 10 and 11 is about what the household does with its door, its table and its words of welcome. He intends the church to have a clear course of action so that confusion does not leave the door open. At the same time the elder never asks them to hate, to harass or to harm. He asks them to stop assisting a ministry that is destroying faith. The first hearers were meant to leave knowing both what to guard and how.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 7 describes. It tells us that deceivers had gone out and that they refused to confess the incarnation. Verses 8 to 11 prescribe. The imperatives are 'watch yourselves,' 'do not receive him' and 'do not greet him,' and they are binding on believers as a pattern of faithfulness. The test of confession in verse 7 and the principle of verse 9 apply to every age, since the incarnation of the Son is the foundation of the gospel in every age.

The application of verses 10 and 11 needs care. The command is given to a house church about a travelling teacher who comes bringing a different teaching. It is not a command about a neighbour, a relative, a colleague, or a sincere seeker who has not yet believed. Jesus sat with sinners and the same apostle's Gospel shows Him speaking to a Samaritan woman, John 4. Nor is it a command about a believer who is struggling and honestly confused. The elder is addressing teachers who bring a message that denies Christ and who expect the church to endorse it. For us today, the principle is that the church must not lend its resources, its pulpit or its name to a message that contradicts the gospel, while continuing to treat every person with the courtesy and love that Jesus showed.

debates.question: How far does the refusal of verses 10 and 11 extend?

views.label: Withholding official welcome from false teachers
views.case: The command concerns a teacher who 'comes to you' bringing a message. Receiving him 'into your home' meant lodging and supporting him, and the greeting meant giving him a hearing as an approved visitor. The elder is forbidding the church to sponsor a ministry that denies Christ, and 3 John shows he does not oppose hospitality as such. This is the reading that best fits the first-century setting.

views.label: A rule for all contact with doctrinal opponents
views.case: Taken at the plain words, 'do not even greet him' seems to ban even civility. Some have used the text to justify cutting off all dealings with anyone who holds a wrong view, and appeal to Paul's instructions about associating with an erring brother, 1 Corinthians 5:11, and about turning away from those who cause divisions, Romans 16:17.

views.label: A rule for gatherings of the church only
views.case: Others emphasise that the home in view is the place where the church meets, and that the refusal applies to giving a false teacher a platform among the believers. Personal conversation with an individual in order to persuade him is not excluded, and the elder in fact hopes to speak face to face with his readers, verse 12.

debates.bearing: The aim is protection of the flock from a message that destroys faith, not a licence for coldness. The first reading is the safest guide. It keeps the force of the command, because the church may not fund or platform a denial of Christ, while leaving room for the love that Jesus commanded in verses 5 and 6, including love for enemies, Matthew 5:44.

debates.question: What does 'the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh' mean, given the present tense?

views.label: The incarnation as a past event with abiding force
views.case: First John 4:2 speaks of Jesus Christ who 'has come in the flesh' with a perfect tense, which stresses a completed act whose result remains. The present participle here may simply describe Jesus as the One who comes in flesh, a settled truth about His identity. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh, and verse 7 is a shorthand for the whole truth of the incarnation.

views.label: A reference to His coming again in the flesh
views.case: A few readers take the present participle to point to the future return, so that the deceivers deny that Jesus will come again in bodily form. The idea is possible grammatically, but 1 John 4:2-3 speaks plainly of a coming that has already happened, so most take verse 7 in the same sense.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that the Son's real bodily existence matters. Most interpreters follow the first view, because the parallel in 1 John makes the incarnation the test. The practical point is the same either way: any teaching that makes Jesus less than truly God and truly man falls under the verdict of verse 7.

debates.question: What is the 'reward' that can be lost in verse 8?

views.label: Fullness of blessing and recognition for faithful labour
views.case: The word means wages, and the elder fears that his readers, and the teachers who laboured among them, could forfeit the full return of their work. Paul speaks of work being tested by fire and of a reward for what survives, with loss for what is burned and yet the person saved, 1 Corinthians 3:13-15.

views.label: Salvation itself
views.case: Some read the warning as a call to keep from losing eternal life, since the next verse says that the one who runs ahead 'does not have God.' On this view the stakes are as high as they can be, and the danger is of abandoning Christ altogether.

debates.bearing: The language of wages fits the first reading better, but verse 9 shows that the danger is not trivial. The elder does not say that believers can earn salvation by labour; he says that the real fruit of the gospel is worth guarding, and that those who leave the teaching of Christ leave God Himself.

study.originalLanguages:
The deceivers 'have gone out,' exelthon, in the aorist tense, a completed departure. The same verb appears in 1 John 2:19, 'They went out from us, but they did not belong to us,' and in 3 John 7 of the faithful workers who 'went out on behalf of the Name.' The verb is shared, but the direction is opposite: some go out under the Name, and some go out from the community. The deceivers are said to refuse to confess 'the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh,' and the negative that governs the participle is me, the negative of description, so that the whole group is characterised by the refusal. 'Coming' is erchomenon, a present participle, and it differs from the perfect tense of 1 John 4:2. John there says Jesus Christ 'has come,' elelythota. The present participle in 2 John may therefore describe the incarnation as a standing truth about who Jesus is. The word 'flesh,' sarx, is the word of John 1:14, which says that the Word became flesh.

The phrase 'the deceiver and the antichrist' carries the article on both nouns, which marks each denier as a representative of the type. The verb behind 'deceiver' is planao, 'lead astray,' and Jesus uses it for the great warning of the last days: 'See to it that no one deceives you,' Matthew 24:4. In Revelation the same family describes the devil as 'the deceiver of the whole world,' Revelation 12:9.

Verse 8 opens with blepete heautous, 'look to yourselves,' a present imperative that calls for a continuing habit of watchfulness. The same pair of words is used by Jesus in Mark 13:9. There is a textual note in the BSB: some early manuscripts read 'what you have worked for' instead of 'what we have worked for,' and the sense shifts slightly from the elder's own labour to the labour of the readers. In either case the loss would be of something real. The reward is misthos plere, 'a full wage,' and the verb apolabete, 'receive,' has the prefix apo, which carries the sense of receiving what is due.

In verse 9 the verb for 'runs ahead' is proago, 'to lead on' or 'go before.' It suggests those who claimed to be advancing beyond the apostolic message, a progress that in fact leaves the path. Some later manuscripts read parabaino, 'transgress,' in place of proago, but the better attested reading is the one that pictures a forward leap. Against it John sets menein, 'remain,' his familiar verb. 'The teaching of Christ' is a phrase whose genitive can be read as the teaching about Christ or the teaching given by Christ, and John may well intend both. The verb echo, 'have,' in 'does not have God,' recurs in 1 John 5:12, 'Whoever has the Son has life.'

The command of verse 10 is a present imperative, 'do not receive,' in a condition that treats the case as real. The phrase 'to greet' is chairein legete, literally 'say rejoice,' the standard form of welcome used at the opening of letters in Acts 15:23 and James 1:1. In verse 11 the verb koinonei, 'shares,' comes from the noun for fellowship, the same word John uses of the church's fellowship with the Father and Son in 1 John 1:3.

typology.type: The false prophet who turns Israel from the LORD, Deuteronomy 13
typology.fulfillment: Moses told Israel that a prophet or dreamer who urged them to follow other gods was to be refused, even if his sign came true, because the LORD was testing whether they loved Him, Deuteronomy 13:1-5. The elder applies the same test to teachers who lead away from the true God as revealed in His Son. In Christ the test becomes the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, 1 John 4:2. The pattern breaks at the penalty: Israel was to put the false prophet to death, but the church is told only to withhold welcome, and its weapons are truth and prayer, 2 Corinthians 10:4.

typology.type: Many antichrists and the one to come
typology.fulfillment: Daniel describes a figure who speaks against the Most High, Daniel 7:25, and Paul speaks of a man of lawlessness who exalts himself above every object of worship, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4. John says that his readers have heard that the antichrist is coming, and that many antichrists have already appeared, 1 John 2:18. The many deceivers of verse 7 are previews of a final enemy, the same opposition in smaller form. The pattern is not finished: the ultimate defeat of the great deceiver comes only when he is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: Hospitality to the messenger as hospitality to the sender
typology.fulfillment: Abraham ran to welcome strangers and entertained the LORD without knowing it, Genesis 18:1-5, and Hebrews 13:2 turns this into a standing rule. Jesus says that whoever receives His messenger receives Him, and receives the One who sent Him, Matthew 10:40. Verses 10 and 11 apply the principle in reverse: to welcome a messenger who denies the Son is to take his side. The pattern shows that hospitality is never morally neutral in the New Testament, since it endorses whom it receives. It falls short as a complete rule because the New Testament also commands kindness to enemies, Matthew 5:44.

study.christ:
The paragraph leads to Christ by making Him the test. Everything in verses 7 to 11 turns on one question: who is Jesus? The false teachers refuse to confess that He came in the flesh, and the elder's response is to say that this is not a side issue but the dividing line between having God and not having Him, verse 9. That is a staggering claim, and it is the claim of the Gospel. 'Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him,' John 5:23. 'No one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him,' Matthew 11:27. If the Son is the only way to the Father, as John 14:6 says, then a teaching that distorts who the Son is leaves the Father unreachable.

It leads to Christ in the incarnation. John 1:14 says that the Word became flesh. John begins his first letter by saying that he and the others had heard, seen and touched the Word of life, 1 John 1:1. The risen Jesus showed His hands and feet and said that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, Luke 24:39. Hebrews says that since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity so that by His death He might destroy the devil, Hebrews 2:14. The flesh is not an incidental covering. Without it there is no death, and without the death there is no atoning sacrifice, 1 John 4:10, no body prepared for the offering, Hebrews 10:5. This is why the elder cares so much. To deny the coming in the flesh is to remove the cross.

It leads to Christ as the teacher. 'The teaching of Christ' can mean the teaching about Him and the teaching that He gave, and Jesus Himself said that His teaching was not His own but the Father's, John 7:16. Remaining in it means staying within the apostolic message that comes from Him and points to Him. Anyone who runs ahead leaves Him behind.

It leads to Christ as the shepherd who guards His own. Jesus says that His sheep will not follow a stranger because they do not recognise his voice, John 10:5. The warnings of the elder are the shepherd's care working through the church, teaching the sheep to know the voice.

A caution is due. The passage must not be turned into a licence for suspicion of every disagreement. Not every different view about baptism, the end times or church order is a denial of the Christ who came in the flesh. The elder applies the sharpest language to the central confession, and that is where the church should be firmest.
study.god:
This paragraph shows a God who cares enough about the truth about Himself to protect it. He is not indifferent to how He is known. The God of the Bible is jealous for His name and for the exclusive worship of His people, Exodus 20:5, and the New Testament carries the same jealousy into the question of who the Son is. A false picture of Jesus is a false picture of the Father, because the Father is known in the Son, Matthew 11:27. That is why the elder says that whoever runs ahead of the teaching of Christ 'does not have God.'

He is a God who gives and keeps. The verse about having 'both the Father and the Son' shows a God who can be possessed, in the sense of known and enjoyed, only through His Son. It is not that people grasp Him but that He gives Himself in the Son to those who remain in the teaching. The gift is real, and what is lost by leaving is real. There are no neutral positions.

He is a God of justice who holds people responsible for what they support. Verse 11 says that whoever greets a false teacher shares in his evil deeds. That is not a doctrine of guilt by accident. It reflects a God who sees the connection between a welcome and a work, and who treats partnership in evil as sharing in it. The same God is the Judge who rewards, as verse 8 says, and Hebrews says that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him, Hebrews 11:6. The God of judgment and the God of reward are one.

He is a God who protects His people through ordinary means. He does not rescue the church from deception by a miracle but by a letter, a test and a practical command. His care comes through the apostolic word and through the church's responsibility to watch itself. The loving shepherd works through the community.

For worship, the paragraph invites believers to confess the incarnate Son as part of their praise and to hold fast to the teaching they have received. A church that sings and prays to the Father and the Son is worshipping the God who is, and in that worship it finds both its security and its guidance for which voices to welcome.

crossReferences.note: John tells believers to test the spirits because many false prophets have gone out into the world, and gives the same test of confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. It is the closest parallel to verse 7 and shows that the two letters address one crisis.

The antichrist is coming and many antichrists have already appeared. They went out from the community, and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father. The passage supplies the background for the language of verses 7 and 9.

Gaius is praised for supporting travelling brothers, while Diotrephes refuses to welcome them. Read beside verses 10 and 11, it shows that the elder values hospitality highly and that the issue is whom the welcome supports.

Jesus warns that many will come in His name and deceive many, and tells His disciples to see to it that no one deceives them. The verb behind deceive is the family of the deceivers in verse 7, and the elder is guarding the church in the very way the Lord asked.

Paul pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches a gospel contrary to the one received. It shows that the apostolic message was fixed and that the church was not free to accept a different one, which is the force of remaining in the teaching of Christ.

Paul warns the Ephesian elders that savage wolves will come in and that men will rise from among their own number to distort the truth. The elder is writing to the same region, and the letter shows this warning being fulfilled.

Israel is told to refuse a prophet who leads away from the LORD, because God is testing their love. The passage is the Old Testament root of the church's duty to test teachers and not to be moved by signs alone.

Paul says that each person's work will be tested by fire, that what survives earns a reward, and that what is burned means loss though the person is saved. It helps to explain the reward of verse 8 as the fruit of faithful work and not the gift of salvation itself.

Paul urges believers to watch out for those who create divisions contrary to the teaching they learned and to turn away from them. It shows that the elder's counsel belonged to a wider apostolic habit of protecting the church from false teachers.

Jesus describes the sheep who will not follow a stranger because they do not know his voice. The passage shows the Good Shepherd's own provision for his flock, and the elder's test of confession is one way the sheep learn to recognise His voice.

The Son shared flesh and blood so that He could die, destroy the devil and become a merciful and faithful high priest. It shows why the incarnation cannot be given up, since the whole work of salvation depends on His real humanity.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God speaking and a serpent contradicting. In Genesis 3 the deceiver asks whether God really said it and then denies what God said, and the whole human race is caught in the lie. From that moment Scripture is the story of true and false words. God sends prophets, and counterfeit prophets arise. He gives a Law with a test for false teachers, Deuteronomy 13, and Israel's history is full of those who led the people astray. The elder's letter belongs to this line, and its warning is the same warning in a late chapter.

The story's answer to the deceiver is the incarnation. The Word who was with God and was God became flesh, John 1:14, and in a human life lived, taught, died and rose. The false teachers of verse 7 strike exactly at this answer, because if the Son did not truly come in the flesh then the rescue has not happened. The elder's insistence is therefore not a footnote to the story but its centre.

The conflict between the truth and the lie does not end in the first century. Jesus predicted that many would come in His name and deceive many, Matthew 24:5, and Paul spoke of a final man of lawlessness, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4. The Revelation names the old serpent as the deceiver of the whole world, Revelation 12:9, and sees him thrown at last into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10. In the meantime the church is called to watch, to hold the teaching and to refuse partnership with what contradicts it. That is what verses 8 to 11 mean in the large story.

The story ends with the lie shut out. In the new creation nothing unclean will enter, nor anyone who practises an abomination or a lie, Revelation 21:27, and the nations will walk in the light of the Lamb. The truth that began in a garden and became flesh in Bethlehem will fill the earth. Until then, the elder's small instruction, to watch yourselves and to stay in the teaching of Christ, is how the church keeps faith with the end it has been promised.

sermon.title: The Danger of Deception
sermon.why: Begg preaches this section, 2 John 1:7-13, on the deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh, the call to abide in the teaching of Christ, and the sober instruction about not aiding false teachers. A clear, orthodox handling of the letter's warning.

quiz.q: What do the deceivers refuse to confess?

options.text: That Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
options.note: Verse 7 makes the incarnation the test; denying it marks the deceiver and antichrist.

options.text: That Jesus was a good moral teacher.
options.note: The denial cuts deeper than morality; it is the reality of the incarnate Son.

options.text: That God exists at all.
options.note: The issue is specifically the coming of Christ in the flesh, not bare theism.

options.text: That Jesus performed miracles.
options.note: Miracles are not the point named; the confession at stake is that the Christ truly came in the flesh.

quiz.q: What does verse 9 say about the teaching of Christ?

options.text: Whoever abides in it has both the Father and the Son; whoever runs beyond it does not have God.
options.note: Verse 9 makes abiding in Christ's teaching the line between having and not having God.

options.text: It is helpful but not essential to knowing God.
options.note: The verse makes it decisive, not optional.

options.text: Only trained teachers need to hold it.
options.note: It is the boundary of faith for all believers, not a specialist concern.

options.text: It can be improved on by advanced thinkers.
options.note: Running ahead beyond it is exactly the danger; it is not to be surpassed but abided in.

quiz.q: What is the best way to understand 'do not receive him into your home or even greet him' in verses 10 and 11?

options.text: Do not host, fund, or endorse travelling teachers who deny Christ, lest you share their work.
options.note: In that culture welcome meant patronage and endorsement of a teacher's mission; this guards against aiding false teaching.

options.text: Never show any courtesy or kindness to anyone who is in error.
options.note: This reads the words too woodenly; the target is endorsing false missionaries, not ordinary civility.

options.text: Refuse all contact with non-Christians of any kind.
options.note: The verses concern Christ-denying teachers seeking a platform, not unbelievers in general.

options.text: Welcome everyone equally regardless of what they teach.
options.note: Hospitality is good, as 3 John shows, but here the elder expressly warns against welcoming those who deny Christ.

quiz.q: How does refusing welcome to false teachers relate to love?

options.text: It is love protecting the flock and the truth from those who would destroy both.
options.note: Guarding believers from soul-destroying error is a faithful form of love, not its opposite.

options.text: It shows that love has limits and sometimes fails.
options.note: It is not a failure of love but love rightly directed toward protecting God's people.

options.text: It proves the elder had abandoned love for harshness.
options.note: The same letter urges love; vigilance and love are held together, not opposed.

options.text: It has nothing to do with love at all.
options.note: The letter binds truth and love, so guarding the truth is an act of love.

quiz.q: Why does the elder call these teachers antichrists?

options.text: Because in denying Christ come in the flesh they stand against and in place of Christ.
options.note: The term names those who oppose the incarnate Son, embodying the spirit of antichrist.

options.text: Because they claimed to be a single final world ruler.
options.note: John uses antichrist of many present deniers, not only a final figure.

options.text: Because they simply disagreed on minor matters.
options.note: The denial strikes the heart of the gospel, not a minor point.

options.text: Because they were political enemies of the church.
options.note: The opposition is doctrinal and spiritual, denying the incarnate Christ, not merely political.

questions: The elder makes the incarnation, Jesus come in the flesh, the test of true teaching. Why does it matter so much that Jesus was truly God and truly human, and how does that shape your hope?
He tells the readers to watch themselves so they do not lose their reward. Where do you most need to be on guard right now so that your faith is not eroded?
To abide in the teaching of Christ is to have both the Father and the Son. What habits help you remain in the truth rather than drifting or running ahead of it?
Refusing to platform false teaching is presented as an act of love, not its opposite. How do you hold together warmth toward people and firmness about the truth in your own relationships and church?

translationNotes.note: The phrase 'coming in the flesh' uses a present participle that can stress the abiding reality of the incarnation, not merely a past event; the deceivers deny that the Christ has genuinely come and remains in the flesh.
A textual variant reads 'that you do not lose what you have worked for' rather than 'what we have worked for', as the BSB footnote notes; the sense of guarding a full reward is unchanged.
'The teaching of Christ' can mean the teaching about Christ or the teaching that comes from Christ; both fit, and the two are inseparable in practice.
'Do not greet him' renders a refusal of the customary welcome-greeting extended to an honoured guest or endorsed teacher, not a blanket ban on all civility.
